source.title: Models, feedback control, and open problems of 3D bipedal robotic walking

accepted.question_text: Develop models, analysis procedures, control designs, and especially stability notions for bipedal locomotion that do not assume the gait is periodic. In particular, characterize and control aperiodic walking behaviors that arise naturally when a biped walks over uneven ground or maneuvers around obstacles.

evidence.quote: The models, analysis procedures and control designs presented in the paper have focused on periodic locomotion. It is important to move beyond this assumption.
There is room for improved notions of stability of aperiodic walking gaits. Two cases where aperiodic gaits arise naturally are walking on uneven ground and maneuvering a biped around obstacles.

accepted.question_text: Determine how to achieve stable bipedal walking on unknown, uneven ground, where the terrain is not flat and may vary significantly. This includes understanding the mechanics, modeling choices, and feedback design needed for robust locomotion when the robot must handle irregular contact conditions rather than the flat-ground case emphasized in the paper.

evidence.quote: This tutorial emphasized walking on flat ground. Much less is known about the problem of bipedal walking on unknown, uneven ground.

accepted.question_text: Develop methods for maneuvering a 3D bipedal robot, such as turning or steering, that come with rigorous stability guarantees and also respect unilateral ground-contact constraints during the maneuver. The goal is not only to generate maneuvers heuristically, but to explain how a robot can change direction safely while maintaining dynamically stable walking.

evidence.quote: Relatively few papers have addressed the issue of maneuvering for bipedal robots, and even fewer have attempted to provide stability guarantees.
How to turn without violating unilateral ground contact constraints is not explained in this work.

accepted.question_text: Find impact models, even approximate ones, for the inelastic collision of the swing leg with the ground that allow a nontrivial double-support phase in robots with stiff feet and limbs. The intended outcome is a hybrid impact model that can represent walking gaits closer to human walking, where double support occupies a significant portion of the gait cycle.

evidence.quote: Work in Miossec and Aoustin [2002] indicates that the approach currently used to represent an inelastic impact of the swing leg with the ground essentially rules out a nontrivial double support phase.
It would be very useful to find impact models, even very approximate ones, that will allow such gaits in robots with “stiff” feet and limbs.

accepted.question_text: Design control methods that let a biped with passive feet or passive ankles stand stably and recover a quiescent standing posture after external pushes. The problem is specifically about balance recovery and stationary stabilization when the ankle is not actively actuated.

evidence.quote: Standing is challenging for robots with passive ankles. Regaining a quiescent standing position after being pushed is even harder.

accepted.question_text: Develop better methods for computing open-loop periodic solutions for hybrid biped models when those solutions must be combined with virtual constraints and, ideally, also satisfy energy-efficiency objectives. The challenge is to avoid the difficulty caused by numerous local minima and to obtain periodic solutions suitable for feedback-law design.

evidence.quote: Our experience is that finding periodic solutions in this manner is difficult due to numerous local minima. The problem is even more difficult when seeking solutions that are energy efficient, in addition to being periodic.
Other approaches to finding periodic orbits, such as those in Srinivasan and Ruina [2006] and Posa et al. [2014], need to be considered when designing feedback laws through virtual constraints.

accepted.question_text: Compute or characterize the domain of attraction of a periodic walking gait for a bipedal robot, especially in the hybrid-systems setting and in the presence of modeling errors that arise when transferring a controller from simulation to the physical robot. The problem asks for practical ways to estimate which perturbations and initial conditions still converge to the desired periodic gait.

evidence.quote: What remains an almost completely unexplored area is computing the domain of attraction for periodic solutions, even for dynamical systems.

Characterizing the domain of attraction of a periodic walking gait for a bipedal robot model is an important consideration with respect to the eventual implementation of the corresponding feedback controller on the actual biped.
There will naturally be errors in the model of the biped, and accounting for these while estimating the domain of attraction would be very useful when passing from simulation to experimentation.

accepted.question_text: Given an anthropomorphic bipedal robot, determine which hybrid model, including the number and nature of its discrete phases, best captures the robot's walking behavior so that stable gaits produced by the model are as human-like as possible. More concretely, identify whether there is a canonical hybrid model for studying controller development for anthropomorphic walking.

evidence.quote: This paper considered two distinct hybrid models. In the literature on bipedal robots, hybrid models have been considered with everywhere from one discrete domain or phase (which is the case for most models considered), to five.

This raises the natural question: given an anthropomorphic bipedal robot, what is the hybrid model that best captures the behavior of this system? In particular, what is the model so that when stable walking gaits are found, these gaits are as human-like as possible?
if a single “most human-like” hybrid model could be found, this could be used as the canonical model for studying controller development for obtaining anthropomorphic walking for bipedal robots.

accepted.question_text: Construct a metric for comparing walking gaits, including a distance between solutions of hybrid systems even when the underlying hybrid models are different, so that one can decide which controller and which hybrid model produce the most human-like walking. Such a metric should also support comparison between robotic walking data and human walking data.

evidence.quote: A question is: which controller for which hybrid model yields the most human-like walking Miura et al. [2011]?

In order to answer this question, a metric on the distance between walking gaits is needed, i.e., a metric for comparing the distance between solutions of hybrid systems even in the case when the hybrid models are different.
This could then be used to both compare different controllers—through a comparison of the resulting periodic solutions—and to compare robotic walking with human walking

accepted.question_text: Develop new cost functions for controller design in bipedal robots that go beyond integral-squared torque per step length and specific cost of transport, using a notion of distance from human-like walking. The objective is to obtain optimization criteria whose minimizers produce periodic gaits that are closer to human walking and therefore potentially more transferable to prosthetic devices.

evidence.quote: Once a viable metric for comparing walking gaits has been found, it can be used to develop new cost-functions.

Yet, currently, there are only two cost functions that are typically considered: the integral-squared torque per step length (as was considered in this paper, see (70)) and the specific cost of transport.
it may be possible to develop better cost functions, i.e., cost functions such that, when minimized, yield periodic solutions that are very “close” to human-like walking gaits.

accepted.question_text: Extend 3D bipedal locomotion modeling and control to robots or prosthetic systems with spherical or otherwise nontrivial foot shapes, and determine how to achieve gait stability when passive or active prostheses are present. This includes the open 3D case of spherical feet and the broader question of stable locomotion with prosthetic components inspired by the rolling behavior of the human ankle-foot system.

evidence.quote: The 3D case is open and interesting.
It would be interesting to extend this work to address gait stability in the presence of passive or active prostheses.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Many other interesting questions arise, ranging from reflex actions to enhance stability under large perturbations, to bipedal robot safety when operating around humans, manipulation of objects, navigation, etc.

evidence.quote: Many other interesting questions arise, ranging from reflex actions to enhance stability under large perturbations, to bipedal robot safety when operating around humans, manipulation of objects, navigation, etc.
